description: We’re a team of CS students from Egyptian Chinese University with backgrounds in data analytics, software engineering, and competitive programming. We love turning real-world data into tools people can actually use, and we’re here to build something meaningful with NASA data and learn a lot along the way.
summary: VitalOrbit is onboard health-monitoring software for astronauts on a Mars mission. Up to 20 light-minutes from Earth, a question to Mission Control and its answer can take up to 40 minutes, so the crew must be its own first responder. VitalOrbit learns each astronaut's personal normal from real wearable heart rate, activity and sleep data, using one machine-learning model per person. It raises an alert only when a problem persists, escalates it and asks the astronaut how they feel. An offline assistant then guides first aid step by step, checking every medicine against the onboard pharmacy and its radiation-shortened expiry. The app also projects NASA's long-mission risks (radiation, bone and muscle loss, eye problems, mental health and cabin CO2) to mission end. Case reports reach the flight surgeon with the real light-time delay applied. In testing it caught 12 of 12 simulated emergencies, with a median of 45 minutes to the first alert and no false critical alarms. Early detection matters because far from Earth, small problems must be caught before they become emergencies.
details: VitalOrbit is onboard health-monitoring software for astronauts on a Mars mission. It addresses the challenge "Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions". On the International Space Station, doctors at Mission Control are seconds away. On Mars, Earth can be up to about 20 light-minutes away (19.1 minutes in our modelled mission), so a question and its answer take about 38 minutes, and during solar conjunction the link is lost for about two weeks. The crew has to be its own first responder. VitalOrbit does four jobs that normally sit with doctors on the ground: It watches. A personal machine-learning model for each astronaut learns that person's own normal heart rate, activity and sleep from real wearable data. It flags readings that are abnormal for that person, not for an average person. It escalates and asks. An alert opens only when a problem persists (30 min, 90 min, 3 h), and the app asks the astronaut how they feel. "I was exercising" closes the alert, and "I don't feel well" opens help. It guides. An offline assistant gives step-by-step first-aid protocols with timers. It checks every suggested medicine against the onboard pharmacy and its radiation-shortened expiry, and it keeps working with no internet and no AI model. It remembers. It projects slow long-mission risks to mission end: radiation dose, bone and muscle loss, eye problems (SANS), mental health and cabin CO2, following NASA's five RIDGE hazards. It sends structured case reports to the flight surgeon with the real light-time delay applied. This matters because on a deep-space mission the window in which a problem is still cheap to fix is short. In our evaluation the system detected 12 of 12 injected emergencies, with a median of 45 minutes to the first alert, no false critical alerts and 0.08 false warnings per crew-day. The same idea applies on Earth wherever the doctor is far away: Antarctic stations, submarines and remote clinics.
